sections.h2: Where is Marion County, Indiana, and how is it organized?
sections.html:
Marion County sits in central Indiana, and its seat is Indianapolis, which is also the state capital. The county covers 403.01 square miles, of which 396.30 are land and 6.71 are water (Wikipedia).

The county was founded on April 1, 1822, and the state capital moved to Indianapolis from Corydon on January 10, 1825. Nine townships make up the map in a three by three grid: Pike, Washington and Lawrence across the top, Wayne, Center and Warren through the middle, and Decatur, Perry and Franklin along the bottom.

City and county government merged in 1970 under a plan known as Unigov. Four places stayed outside it as excluded municipalities: Beech Grove, Lawrence, Southport and the town of Speedway. Several small included towns, such as Clermont, Homecroft and Williams Creek, keep limited local authority. School districts and fire districts were never merged into the consolidated government.

For an owner this matters because a Marion County tax bill can carry levies from more than one layer of local government, depending on which township, school district and municipality the parcel sits in.

sections.h2: What does Marion County property tax cost and who sets it?
sections.html:
Marion County does not have a single flat rate. Each parcel sits in a taxing district, and the district rate is applied to the assessed value after deductions and credits. The Treasurer publishes a "Review Tax Rates" page on indy.gov where you can look up the rate for a given year.

Three separate bodies touch your bill:

  • The Marion County Assessor sets assessed values and takes appeals.
  • The Marion County Auditor handles homestead and other deductions. The Recorder's deed page points owners to the Auditor for the standard homestead and mortgage deductions.
  • The Marion County Treasurer bills, collects and distributes the money.

Indiana changed the homestead rules in 2025. According to a May 2026 memo from the Department of Local Government Finance, the standard homestead deduction is $40,000 for the 2026 assessment date, down from $48,000, and it steps down by $10,000 each year until it ends with the 2030 assessment date. The supplemental deduction percentage rises over the same period, to 46 percent for taxes payable in 2027. A Purdue Extension summary adds a new supplemental homestead credit of 10 percent of the bill, up to $300, starting in 2026.

If you are selling, these changes mostly affect the buyer. A new owner has to file for their own homestead deduction after closing, so the bill you paid may not match the bill they receive.

sections.h2: What are the key Marion County property tax dates and offices?
sections.html:
Marion County property tax is due May 11 and November 10 in 2026, and payments go to the Treasurer's Office in the City-County Building. The table below lists the facts the county publishes.

ItemDetail
2026 due datesMay 11 and November 10
Treasurer200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001, Indianapolis, IN 46204; (317) 327-4444
Treasurer hours8 AM to 4:30 PM Monday to Friday; 8 AM to 5:30 PM on Nov 6, 9 and 10
Closed daysNov 3 (Election Day) and Nov 11 (Veterans Day)

Assessor branch offices7128 Waldemar Drive (North); 501 N Post Rd, Suite D (East)

The Treasurer's Office says owners can pay online, by phone, by mail, in person or at a bank, and can schedule recurring payments through an account login. Paperless statements are also available.

sections.h2: How do penalties work if a Marion County bill is paid late?
sections.html:
A late payment adds 5 percent of the unpaid tax if you pay within 30 days of the due date and have no prior-year balance on the parcel. If the tax and penalty are not paid within those 30 days, the penalty becomes 10 percent (Indiana DLGF).

A short delay can therefore cost real money on a larger bill. On a $3,000 half-year installment, 5 percent is $150 and 10 percent is $300.

Past a certain point the county can place the parcel in a tax sale. Marion County places a lien on homes with unpaid taxes and auctions the lien online. The 2026 sale ran October 13 through 16. To stop a parcel from being sold, an owner had to pay all unpaid taxes, penalties and special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, plus a $325 tax sale administration fee, by October 8, 2026 at 4:30 PM. The county accepts cash, certified checks, cashier's checks or money orders for that payment, and does not take personal or business checks.

The Treasurer's site lists a tax sale payment plan, partial payments and paying after a sale as separate topics, so ask the office what applies to your parcel.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Marion County assessment?
sections.html:
You file a written appeal, Form 130, with the assessing official, which in Marion County is the Assessor. Under the state's November 2025 fact sheet, the deadline is June 15 of the year the tax bill is mailed when the county sent the notice of assessment after May 1, and June 15 of the assessment year when it sent the notice earlier.

After filing, the Assessor holds an informal meeting. If that does not settle it, the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals must hold a hearing within 180 days of the petition. A further appeal goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131.

A pending appeal can lower what you owe in the meantime. The state fact sheet says you may pay based on the prior year's assessment while the appeal is pending, without penalty. A law firm note from April 2026 says Indiana Code 6-1.1-15-10 applies this rule and recommends sending the Treasurer a written explanation with the payment. The difference is not erased, though. If the appeal fails, you owe it.

Recent assessment activity in Marion County has been heavy. The same law firm reported that the Assessor added nearly $5.5 billion of assessed value to Indianapolis commercial and industrial property for the January 1, 2025 assessment date.

The Assessor also posted a notice that owners hurt by recent flooding may ask for a review by submitting Form 137R, and a disaster reassessment petition is listed among its services.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax bill when you sell a house in Marion County?
sections.html:
The seller owes the taxes for the period they owned the house, and the title company usually settles this at closing. Indiana taxes are paid after the year they cover, so a spring or fall installment can still be unpaid on closing day.

Before listing or accepting an offer, it helps to gather these items:

  • The latest tax statement and the parcel number.
  • Proof that the last installment was paid, or the amount still owed.
  • Any pending Form 130 appeal, since it changes what the bill should be.
  • Notice of any tax sale list status, which the Treasurer can confirm.

The transfer itself runs through the Assessor first. Deeds and sales disclosures must be stamped at Room W121, with a $10 transfer fee per parcel and $20 per sales disclosure form, and then the stamped deed goes to the Recorder, where the fee is $35 per document (indy.gov). The Assessor asks owners to build the sales disclosure in the Properly online system.

A house with back taxes, a lien or a stalled estate can be hard to sell on the open market. Marion County owners in that position often look at selling as-is so that the unpaid amount is taken from the sale price rather than paid up front.

sections.h2: What is the climate and economy like in Marion County?
sections.html:
Marion County has hot summers and cold winters, so roofs, gutters and heating systems get a full workout. Recent January averages sit near 20 degrees Fahrenheit and July near 86. The record low is minus 22 (January 1985) and the record high is 104 (June 1988). Monthly precipitation runs from about 2.05 inches in January to 4.78 inches in July (Wikipedia).

The county economy is large. Wikipedia reports a total GDP of $135.593 billion for 2024. Indianapolis International Airport and Eagle Creek Airpark are both in the county.

The median home here was built in 1972, per the Census figures already shown above, so many houses are past the age where roofs, furnaces and sewer lines need replacing. Condition is a common reason owners decide to sell as-is instead of repairing.

faqs.q: When is the next Marion County property tax due?
faqs.a: The Marion County Treasurer lists two 2026 due dates: May 11 and November 10. The office will have extended hours of 8 AM to 5:30 PM on November 6, 9 and 10, and it is closed on November 3 and November 11.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Marion County property tax in person?
faqs.a: Go to the Treasurer's Office in the City-County Building, 200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001, Indianapolis. Regular hours are 8 AM to 4:30 PM, Monday to Friday. You can also call (317) 327-4444.

faqs.q: How late can I file a Marion County assessment appeal?
faqs.a: The state's fact sheet gives June 15 as the filing deadline for Form 130, tied to the year the tax bill is mailed or the assessment year, depending on when the notice went out. Confirm the date for your notice with the Assessor at (317) 327-4907.

faqs.q: Can I stop a Marion County tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, before the sale. For 2026 the owner had to pay all unpaid taxes, penalties, special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees and a $325 administration fee by October 8, 2026 at 4:30 PM. Contact the Treasurer for what applies after that date.

faqs.q: Who stamps a deed in Marion County before it is recorded?
faqs.a: The Marion County Assessor does, in Room W121 of the City-County Building. The stamped deed then goes to the Recorder's Office. Fees at the Assessor are $10 per parcel and $20 for a sales disclosure when one is required.

faqs.q: Do I owe property tax if the house sells before the bill arrives?
faqs.a: Usually the sellers' share is settled at closing through the title company, since Indiana bills in arrears. Ask the title company to confirm both installments for the parcel and any amounts still open.
